scenario.description: A litigation director must approve the company's initial defense plan in a trade-secret lawsuit, including the scope of discovery, protective relief, counsel selection, insurance conditions, and forensic work, with input from discovery counsel and the firm's insurance-coverage specialist.

shared_context.S1: The company has been sued by a former employee for alleged misappropriation of trade secrets, and the complaint seeks broad inspection of company devices and systems.
shared_context.S2: The court has set an initial case-management conference for next month, and no discovery has yet been exchanged.
shared_context.S3: The company wants to protect its confidential information while keeping the defense costs controlled.
shared_context.S4: As part of the firm's standard litigation-planning meeting, Elena asks discovery counsel and insurance-coverage counsel to identify any facts that should shape the initial defense plan before she approves it; Elena may approve the plan with commitments to resolve administrative or coverage follow-up items after the meeting.

PF1.text: Samir's forensic review of the former employee's company laptop confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied, found no customer data on the device, and found no evidence of any additional copying; his report is awaiting final partner review and has not been added to the case plan.

PF2.text: Morgan reviewed the applicable policy endorsement and confirmed that the trade-secret defense is covered subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention, insurer-approved panel counsel, written insurer consent before any forensic vendor is engaged, and notification to the insurer as part of the approved defense plan; the endorsement is stored in the risk department's file and has not been attached to this matter.

acceptance_conditions: The defense plan must seek a narrow protective order rather than accept broad inspection.
Discovery must be limited to the exactly three identified trade-secret files.
The plan must not require production of customer data.
The defense must use insurer-approved panel counsel.
The client must be assigned exactly a $75,000 self-insured retention.
Any forensic vendor engagement must require written insurer consent.
The plan must require notification to the insurer.
The plan must include an insurer-notification commitment.

content_checks.C4: 'insurer-approved panel counsel' in decisions['counsel_model'] or 'panel counsel' in decisions['counsel_model']
content_checks.C8: any('Notify the insurer' in c['detail'] or 'notify the insurer' in c['detail'] or 'notification to the insurer' in c['detail'] or 'insurer notification' in c['detail'] or 'reach out to the insurer' in c['detail'] or 'initiate contact with the insurer' in c['detail'] for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: The forensic count changes the response from broad inspection to a protective order covering exactly three files, and the absence of customer data changes customer-data production from required to prohibited.

The policy endorsement changes counsel selection to insurer-approved panel counsel, sets the client retention at exactly $75,000, requires written insurer consent for forensic work, and adds insurer notification as an explicit plan requirement.
